cards.title: Three random words
cards.body: The NCSC suggests building passwords from three random words, such as kettlecactusbanjo. Long and unexpected beats short and clever, and it's easier to remember. Skip birthdays, pet names and football teams, which are often on social media. Swapping letters for numbers, like a zero for an o, adds little because criminals know that trick.

quiz.q: What does the NCSC say about swapping letters for numbers, like 0 for o?
options: It adds little, as criminals know the trick
quiz.explain: Simple swaps don't make passwords much stronger, but they do make them harder for you to remember.

source.name: NCSC: Three random words

cards.title: Guard the email account first
cards.body: Email is the master key: it's where password resets go. If a criminal gets in, they can reset other accounts and send messages pretending to be you. The NCSC says to give email its own strong password, used nowhere else, and change it straight away if it's been reused. Then do the same for banking and shopping.

source.name: NCSC: Use a strong and separate password for your email

cards.title: Let a password manager remember
cards.body: A password manager keeps your passwords behind one main password, so every account can have its own. Many will create strong passwords and only fill them in on the genuine website, which helps against fake sites. The NCSC suggests turning on two-step verification for the manager too, and using passkeys wherever a site offers them.

quiz.q: Why does a password manager's autofill help protect against phishing?
options: It hides your screen from others
It changes your password every day
It only fills in on the correct website
quiz.explain: A password manager recognises the real site, so it won't fill your details into a lookalike page.

source.name: NCSC: Password managers

cards.title: A second lock on the door
cards.body: Two-step verification, also called 2FA, adds a second check when you sign in, such as a code by text, an authenticator app or a fingerprint. Even if someone has the password, they can't get in without it. The NCSC says start with email, then banking, social media and shopping. You're usually only asked when something looks unusual.

source.name: NCSC: Turn on 2-step verification

cards.title: Stop, Challenge, Protect
cards.body: The Take Five campaign has a simple rhythm. Stop: take a moment before handing over money or details. Challenge: could it be fake? It's fine to refuse, reject or ignore a request, and feeling rushed is a red flag. Protect: if you think you've been scammed, contact your bank straight away and report it.

quiz.q: In Take Five's advice, what's a warning sign that a request could be a scam?
quiz.explain: Criminals create urgency so you don't stop to think. Genuine organisations won't mind you taking a moment.

source.name: Take Five to Stop Fraud

cards.title: Hang up and call 159
cards.body: Unexpected call about your money? Hang up and dial 159. It connects you to your own bank on a number that can't be faked, and covers customers of more than 99% of UK current accounts. Use it whenever a caller claims to be your bank, the police or a fraud team. A genuine bank won't mind at all.

options: Reports a crime to the police
Connects you safely to your own bank
quiz.explain: 159 puts you through to your bank so you can check whether an unexpected call about money was genuine.

source.name: Stop Scams UK: 159

cards.title: What your bank will never ask
cards.body: Age UK's reminders: banks won't ask for your PIN or send a courier for your card. Police won't ask you to help an investigation using your card details. HMRC won't cold-call for bank details. Scammers can keep a landline open after you hang up, so call back on a different phone, or wait 10 to 15 minutes.

source.name: Age UK: Phone scams and cold calls

cards.title: Courier fraud
cards.body: It starts with a call from "the bank" or "the police" about a problem with your account. Then a courier is sent to collect your card, PIN, cash or gold. Banks and police never do this, and never ask you to lie to your bank. Hang up, keep your valuables, don't open the door, and tell someone you trust.

quiz.q: Will a real bank or police force send a courier to collect your card?
options: Yes, if there's fraud on the account
Only if you give them a password first
quiz.explain: Banks and police never collect cards, PINs, cash or valuables. Hang up and call your bank on a number you trust.

source.name: Take Five: Courier scams

cards.title: Stop, Lock, Chain, Check
cards.body: Age UK's routine for an unexpected knock: are you expecting anyone? Lock the back door first, as some scammers work in pairs. Use the chain and peephole. Check ID by ringing the company on a number from a bill, not one they give you. Never sign or pay on the spot, and it's fine to say no.

source.name: Age UK: Doorstep scams

cards.title: Romance scams
cards.body: Romance scammers often move fast: declaring love within days, wanting to leave the dating site, dodging video calls, and sooner or later needing money for an emergency or a ticket to visit. They may ask you to keep things secret. Age UK's rule is simple: never send money to someone you haven't met in person, whatever the story.

quiz.q: What is Age UK's rule about sending money to an online love interest?
options: Never send money to someone you haven't met in person
Send it by bank transfer, not cash
quiz.explain: However convincing the story, Age UK says never send money to someone you haven't met face to face.

source.name: Age UK: How to spot a catfish

cards.title: HMRC won't text you a rebate
cards.body: HMRC never texts about a tax rebate, and won't use social media to offer one or ask for your details. Genuine HMRC emails come from addresses ending hmrc.gov.uk. Forward suspicious HMRC emails to phishing@hmrc.gov.uk and texts to 60599, and report odd calls through GOV.UK. If in doubt, check HMRC's list of genuine contacts.

source.name: GOV.UK: Report HMRC phishing emails, texts and phone call scams

cards.title: If it's happened: bank, then report
cards.body: Lost money or details to a scam? Contact your bank first, using the number on your card, your banking app or 159. Then report it to Report Fraud on 0300 123 2040, or call 101 in Scotland. If you feel in danger, dial 999. Scammers rely on secrecy, so tell someone you trust. It happens to clever people every day.

source.name: Take Five: Courier scams

cards.title: LPAs: the two types
cards.body: A lasting power of attorney lets someone you trust make decisions if you can't (England and Wales). Property and financial affairs covers bills, bank accounts, pensions and selling a home, and can be used once registered, with permission. Health and welfare covers care, medical treatment and where you live, and only applies when you can't decide yourself.

quiz.q: When can a health and welfare LPA be used?
options: Only when the person can't make the decision themselves
Only after the person has died
quiz.explain: A health and welfare LPA only applies when the donor lacks capacity. A financial LPA can be used sooner, with permission.

source.name: GOV.UK: Lasting power of attorney

cards.title: Registering an LPA
cards.body: An LPA has to be registered with the Office of the Public Guardian before it can be used. As of November 2026 it costs £92 per LPA, so £184 for both types. You may pay less on an income under £12,000, or nothing on certain benefits. Registration takes 8 to 10 weeks if there are no mistakes, so don't leave it late.

quiz.q: As of November 2026, what does it cost to register one LPA?
quiz.explain: GOV.UK lists £92 per LPA, so £184 for both types. Reductions or exemptions may apply on low income or certain benefits.

source.name: GOV.UK: Register a lasting power of attorney

cards.title: Why sooner beats later
cards.body: If someone loses mental capacity without an LPA, family may need to apply to the Court of Protection to become a deputy. That means a court process, a fee, and an annual report to the Office of the Public Guardian about decisions made. An LPA can only be made while the person still has capacity, which is why it's worth doing early.

source.name: GOV.UK: Become a deputy

cards.title: Give your will a check-up
cards.body: GOV.UK suggests reviewing a will every five years and after big changes, like separation, a new baby, moving house or an executor dying. In England and Wales, getting married cancels a will made before. A signed will can't be scribbled on: changes need a properly witnessed codicil, or for bigger changes, a new will.

quiz.q: In England and Wales, what happens to an existing will when you get married?
quiz.explain: Marriage cancels any will made before it, so it's worth making a new one afterwards.

source.name: GOV.UK: Making a will, update your will

cards.title: Where's the will?
cards.body: A will only helps if someone can find it. GOV.UK says you can keep it at home or store it with a solicitor, your bank, a will storage company or the national probate registry. Whichever you choose, tell your executor and a close friend or relative where it is. Note the location, not the contents, in your family records.

source.name: GOV.UK: Making a will, write your will

cards.title: Tell Us Once
cards.body: After a death is registered, the registrar can give you a Tell Us Once reference. It lets you tell most government bodies in one go, including HMRC, DWP, the Passport Office, DVLA and the local council. Use it within 28 days. It covers England, Scotland and Wales, and you'll still need to contact banks, insurers and utilities yourself.

quiz.q: How long do you have to use a Tell Us Once reference number?
quiz.explain: The reference expires after 28 days, and the registrar may not issue another, so it's worth using promptly.

source.name: GOV.UK: Tell Us Once

cards.title: Apple Legacy Contact
cards.body: Apple lets you choose a Legacy Contact who can ask for access to things like photos, messages, notes and backups after you die. Set it up in Settings under Sign-In & Security. It creates an access key they'll need, along with a death certificate. They won't get passwords, payment details or purchased films and music. Keep the key with your important papers.

source.name: Apple Support: How to add a Legacy Contact

cards.title: Your emergency info sheet
cards.body: If paramedics arrived, what would they need? The Message in a Bottle form makes a good template: name, allergies, medical conditions and medication, GP details, two emergency contacts, and anyone you care for. A copy of the repeat prescription list helps too. Keep it to one page, date it, and update it whenever medication changes.

source.name: North East Ambulance Service: Message in a bottle

cards.title: Google's Inactive Account Manager
cards.body: Google's Inactive Account Manager lets you decide what happens if your account goes quiet for a period you choose. You can pick up to 10 trusted people to be told, or to download chosen data like photos or emails. Without a plan, Google may delete an account that's been inactive across Google for at least two years.

source.name: Google Account Help: Inactive Account Manager

cards.title: Keep a medication list
cards.body: Age UK suggests keeping an up-to-date list of every medicine taken, including over-the-counter and herbal ones, not just prescriptions. Take it to appointments and hospital stays. Don't stop a medicine suddenly without talking to a GP or pharmacist. If someone takes lots of medicines, ask whether they could have a free NHS structured medication review.

quiz.q: What should a medication list include, according to Age UK?
quiz.explain: Over-the-counter and herbal products can interact with prescriptions, so everything taken belongs on the list.

source.name: Age UK: Getting the most from your medicines

cards.title: Message in a Bottle
cards.body: Message in a Bottle is a free scheme run with Lions Clubs. Fill in the form with key medical details and contacts, put it in the bottle and keep it in the fridge door. One sticker goes on the fridge, the other inside the front door, so paramedics know to look. Kits come from GP surgeries, pharmacies and local Lions clubs.

quiz.q: Where should a Message in a Bottle be kept?
options: In the fridge, ideally the door
quiz.explain: Emergency crews know to check the fridge when they spot the stickers on the front door and fridge.

source.name: North East Ambulance Service: Message in a bottle

cards.title: Cut down cold calls
cards.body: Registering with the Telephone Preference Service is free and should cut cold calls, though not every scammer respects it. Age UK also suggests answerphones, your phone's call blocking, or a separate call blocker; some councils provide them. Forward scam texts to 7726. And remember, caller ID can be faked, so a familiar number isn't proof.

quiz.q: Does registering with the Telephone Preference Service stop all scam calls?
options: Yes, it blocks every unknown number
No, it reduces cold calls but not every scammer
quiz.explain: TPS cuts legitimate cold calls, but criminals ignore it, so stay alert and use call blocking too.

source.name: Age UK: Phone scams and cold calls

cards.title: Forward the dodgy email
cards.body: Don't click links in a suspicious email. Forward it to the NCSC's Suspicious Email Reporting Service at report@phishing.gov.uk. It's free, and you can send as many as you like, even if you're not sure. That isn't the same as reporting a crime, though: if you've lost money, contact your bank and Report Fraud.

source.name: NCSC: Report a scam email

cards.title: Say yes to updates
cards.body: Those "update available" pop-ups are worth tapping. The NCSC calls installing updates one of the most important and quickest things you can do, because they protect against viruses and malware. Turn on automatic updates, do big ones at home on Wi-Fi with the device plugged in, and watch for older phones that no longer get updates.

quiz.q: Why does the NCSC say to install updates promptly?
options: They make the battery last longer
They protect against viruses and malware
quiz.explain: Updates close security gaps. Devices that no longer receive them miss out on those fixes.

source.name: NCSC: Install the latest software and app updates

cards.title: Back up the photos
cards.body: Phones get lost, laptops die, and ransomware can lock files. The NCSC suggests backing up anything you'd miss, to the cloud, a removable drive, or both. Unplug drives when you're not using them, protect cloud accounts with two-step verification, and now and then check a backup actually restores. For family photos, keep copies in two places.

source.name: NCSC: Back up your data

cards.title: Choosing attorneys
cards.body: Choose attorneys you trust to act in your best interests. They must be 18 or over, and you can appoint more than one, plus replacements. You'll also need a certificate provider, who confirms you understand the LPA and aren't being pressured. Age UK says they must have known you well for two years, or be a professional such as a doctor.

quiz.q: What does an LPA certificate provider confirm?
options: That you understand the LPA and aren't under pressure
That your attorneys are rich enough
quiz.explain: The certificate provider is a safeguard, checking you understand what you're signing and haven't been pushed into it.

source.name: Age UK: Power of attorney

cards.title: Ordinary power of attorney
cards.body: An ordinary power of attorney isn't the same as an LPA. It only covers financial decisions and only works while you still have mental capacity, so it suits short-term needs like a hospital stay or a long trip. Age UK says an LPA is usually the better choice if you might lose capacity later. Get advice, as there's no standard form.

source.name: Age UK: Power of attorney

cards.title: One step at a time
cards.body: GOV.UK's guide to what to do when someone dies breaks it into steps: register the death, tell government (Tell Us Once helps), arrange the funeral, check for bereavement benefits and help with costs, value the estate, and apply for probate if needed. Nobody has to do it all at once, and bereavement support is there too.

source.name: GOV.UK: What to do when someone dies
